title: Competitive markets and living standards
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:37Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: None of the bank points teaches the link between competitive markets and rising living standards: competition policy covers the law against anti-competitive conduct, market structures covers types of market power, and the business card covers types of markets, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Competitive markets and living standards
card: When many firms compete for customers, each must keep its price low or lose sales to rivals.
Firms also compete on quality. A firm with poor products or service can lose customers to a better rival.
Competition drives new ideas. Firms that find cheaper methods or better products can win more sales.
Lower prices, better quality and new ideas mean resources flow to the goods people value most. Households can then buy more and better goods, so living standards can rise.
draft.remember: Competition pushes firms to cut prices, lift quality and innovate, which can raise living standards.

a.q: Three phone repair shops open in the same Geelong street and compete for customers. What is the most likely effect on customers?
opts: Lower prices or better service
Higher prices for the same service
Fewer shops to choose from
Slower repairs as shops share work
a.why: Each shop must offer a better deal or lose customers to the others, so prices tend to fall or service improves. Higher prices would suit a shop with no rivals, not one facing competition.
a.clue: Customers can walk to a rival.

b.q: Why can strong competition between supermarkets raise living standards?
opts: Households can buy more and better goods for their income
Firms can charge more because they have more customers
Governments can set all prices more easily
Households spend less on goods they value most
b.why: Lower prices and better quality let households get more from their income, which raises living standards. Higher prices would reduce what households can buy. Competition works through the market, not government price setting.
b.clue: Think about what falling prices do to what income can buy.

b.best: Households can buy more and better goods for their income

problems.detail: The clue ('what falling prices do to what income can buy') points straight at the only option that mentions buying and income, so a student can match words without knowing the idea.
Very easy for Year 12. The three wrong options (higher prices, slower repairs, fewer shops) are plainly the opposite of what the stem describes, and the clue adds a further hint.

proposal.title: Competitive markets and living standards
card: When many firms compete for customers, each must keep its price low or lose sales to rivals.
Firms also compete on quality. A firm with poor products or service can lose customers to a better rival.
Competition drives new ideas. Firms that find cheaper methods or better products can win more sales.
Firms that offer what buyers value win sales and grow, while others shrink. Resources flow to the goods people value most, and households can buy more and better goods, so living standards can rise.
proposal.remember: Competition pushes firms to cut prices, lift quality and innovate, which can raise living standards.

a.q: Two cafés in Bendigo compete. Café A offers better coffee at the same price and wins customers from Café B. What does this show?
opts: Resources shift toward the product buyers value more
Competition lowers quality as cafés chase sales
Buyers lose out because one of the cafés shrinks
Café A can now raise prices with no risk of losing sales
a.why: Buyers move their spending to the coffee they value more, so Café A grows and Café B shrinks. Resources follow buyers toward what they value. Café B shrinking is not a loss to buyers, and Café A still faces a rival, so it cannot raise prices without risk.
a.clue: Which café can now afford more staff and beans?

b.q: Why can strong competition between supermarkets raise living standards?
opts: Lower prices let each dollar of income buy more
Higher prices give supermarkets more to reinvest
Fewer brands on shelves make shopping simpler
Government price controls keep grocery costs fixed
b.why: Rivals must keep prices low or lose sales, so a household's income buys more goods, which raises living standards. Higher prices would cut what households can buy. Competition works through the market, not through government price setting.
b.clue: Competition acts on firms first. What does it push them to do?

a.best: Resources shift toward the product buyers value more

b.best: Lower prices let each dollar of income buy more
